messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the great advice and example!

I also wanted to know if there is a way to include random effects in a distance model. The data I am working on was collect by over 20 different observers. That is too many to include observer as a fixed effect and the model will just crash. Thus, maybe a random effect could be a solution so that I can account for observer effect in the model. Any ideas?

Thank you again!

All my best,
Bastien Dehaudt

On Friday, September 27, 2024 at 4:45:34 PM UTC+10 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> Bastien
>
> You could treat years as "strata" in your analysis. However, the question to answer is whether detectability differs between years.  An example of addressing this question for stratified data is shown here:
>
> https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-strata/strata-distill.html
>
> You should also note the answer I just gave to Nilanjan regarding his 12 years of data from India. I suggested a third approach for him whereby year could be treated as a covariate in a single detection function model to account for yearly variation in detectability.
> From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Bastien Dehaudt <bdeh...@gmail.com>
> Sent: 27 September 2024 05:38
> To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: {Suspected Spam} Re: [distance-sampling] Trail transect distance analysis
>
> Thank you, this is really helpful!
>
> I have another question. If I want to look at changes in relative density between each of the 8 years, does this mean I need to fit a different ds() model for each year of the survey? And then plot the result of the model for each year on a graph (x-axis=year, y-axis=estimated relative density). Or is it possible to run it all in a single model which will give a density estimate for each year? The goal is to look at trends in populations across time. I am using the distance package in R.
>
> Thank you for all your help!
> All my best,
> Bastien Dehaudt
> On Wednesday, September 25, 2024 at 5:02:29 PM UTC+10 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Welcome Bastien
> >
> > Conducting distance sampling surveys along trails creates two problems, neither related to curvature of the trails. First, trails are not placed randomly through the habitat, making extrapolation dubious from the vicinity of the trails to the larger area. Second, animals know where the trails are located; they are either attracted or repelled by the trail violating the assumption that animals area evenly distributed with respect to distance from the trail out to the truncation distance.
> >
> > By combining transects into a single transect, you lose spatial replication hence cannot estimate variability in encounters between transects. This then negates the ability to make inference from the trails to the wider area. But if it is relative change you wish to measure, perhaps you are content with this price to pay. In which case, you can analyse the data in the manner you describe; mindful of the caveats I mentioned.
> >
> > Monthly surveys over eight years results in nearly 100 months. You might consider combining data across three or four months to increase sample size for each of the surveys.
> > From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Bastien Dehaudt <bdeh...@gmail.com>
> > Sent: 25 September 2024 05:05
> > To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> > Subject: [distance-sampling] Trail transect distance analysis
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am trying to analyses a dataset using distance but the method design is a bit untraditional and I would love to receive advice on how to go about it.
> >
> > A group of connected trails were walked roughly twice per month and an observer recorded detections of various wildlife species (vocal and visual) and estimated the distance and angle of this detection. I have attached a screenshot of the map of the trails to this email. We have about 8 years of such data and we are interested in looking at trends in populations over time. Because the transects follow trails, they are not straight and so we are only able to look at relative abundance, not estimate absolute abundance. Thankfully, the method remain pretty much the same over the 8 year period.
> >
> > Because there are errors in the dataset with the trail names (change throughtout the years + human error) and trails were sometimes walked more or less than twice during a month, I want to treat each month as 1 single transect with length equal to the length of all the trails walked that month. Thus, its length essentially represents the walking effort for that month. Is it possible to conduct a distance analysis by feeding it data that is presented as 1 transect per month with a different length each month? Remember, we are only interested in changes in relative abundance over time, but we would like to use distance to be able to account for observer effect and detection probability.
> >
> > Please let me know what you think, how you would go about it, or if you would like any clarifications.
> >
> > Thank you for your help!
> > All my best,
> > Bastien Dehaudt
> >

messages.subject: Re: effort misunderstanding
messages.subject_clean: effort misunderstanding
messages.body_plain:
To add another question for the same R script (above was talking about input file for ds), for my dht2 output the 'Area' is coming out as the individual area for each region whereas the 'CoveredArea' is presented as the total, meaning my abundance estimates are lower than the actual sample since the covered area is greater than the total.

On Monday, September 30, 2024 at 12:25:26 PM UTC-6 Rebecca wrote:
> Hi there,
> I have carried out a point count survey with 4 points in different areas (1 point per area) and each point was visited 80 times. I thus put the effort for each observation as 80 but the covered area has been calculated as the area covered by the point multiplied by 80. It looks like R has assumed I have covered 80 different points per area but only 4 points were covered and just visited 80 times meaning the covered area is 80x too large. How to I fix this so that the repeat measurements are accounted for but the covered area is not multiplied by the effort?
> Thank you,
> Rebecca

> I believe I am having a similar issue. I am carrying out a point transect survey with 4 points, each visited 80 times. I put my effort for each observation as 80 but the covered area has been calculated by multiplying the area of each point by 80 - I assume this is because it is assuming I have sampled 80 points per area (4 areas) whereas each area is only 1 point and repeats were at the same location meaning the covered area is 80x too large.

> Thank you,
> Rebecca

> On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 2:02:07 AM UTC-6 er26 wrote:
> > Exactly right Cali.  The "Survey effort" field is a mandatory field (visits for points, line length for transects).  Distance MUST have that information because it is "hard wired" into Distance's calculations.  Therefore, you need not explicitly "point" to that field, Distance looks for it automatically.
> >
> >
> > On 02/10/2015 08:56, Lisa Cali Crampton wrote:
> > > hi Eric, thanks for the quick replay.
> > >
> > > So if I understand what you're saying, simply by specifying survey effort in the data import stage, I've done all I need to do. I don't need to refer to that column indicating survey effort in any of the further model input windows. Is that right? Great!
> > >
> > > Thanks
> > > Cali
> > >
> > > On Thu, Oct 1, 2015 at 9:46 PM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> > > > Cali
> > > >
> > > > Not sure I understand your question.  Sounds like you've set up your project properly.  You have recorded number of visits in the "Survey effort" field of the transect layer along with covariates (including visit number) at the observation layer.
> > > >
> > > > Distance calculates encounter rate as the number of detections per unit of effort (visit).  Consequently by specifying 3 visits to the point, Distance calculates the proper encounter rate.  There is no need for the number of visits to be equal for all points.  Perhaps on one visit, you were unable to get to some of the points, therefore the number of detections on those points will be a function of 2 visits rather than 3; you merely indicate "Survey effort" of 2 for those points.
> > > >
> > > > Your analysis will not model survey effort (it is known and not estimated), but the number of detections is a function of effort; that is taken into account in the manner I described.
> > > >
> > > > On 02/10/2015 02:50, ca...@kauaiforestbirds.org wrote:
> > > > > hi all, I've seen several related posts but so far none that answer my question.
> > > > >
> > > > > We have made three visits over the course of several weeks to each of 30 point count stations, where we performed an 8-minute count on each visit.
> > > > >
> > > > > We have imported all of the data into Distance, accounting for the three repeat visits as "survey effort" at the "point transect" level. So for each point, we have the name of the point, and the survey effort = 3. Then at the sample level, we have each observation with its distance, as well as covariates relating to the time and weather of each visit, and the visit number (1-3).
> > > > >
> > > > > My question is: where in the modeling phase (the "inputs") do we bring the survey effort in? i.e., where do we tell Distance that we have repeated counts at each station, as opposed to all of those observations coming from a single visit.
> > > > >
> > > > > I understand that the point may be moot because we have equal numbers of visits at all stations....but even if so, for the future, when that is likely to not be the case, I'd like to know how to model survey effort.
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks!
> > > > > Cali

messages.body_plain:
Thomas

Can you provide more information regarding what you want? The gz function returns a probability. Subsequent code calculates effective strip width. What do you want?
From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Thomas Webber <webber...@gmail.com>
Sent: 30 September 2024 18:46

To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] p and esw for each value of covariat

Hi Eric,

Following on further from the previous posts, I am trying to update your gz function to work with point data as opposed line transect data, though I'm not managing to get very far. I wondered if you would be able to help at all?

Best,
Thomas

On Saturday 13 May 2023 at 08:03:50 UTC-4 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> Tim
>
> Thanks for double-checking the code. Indeed the code did have a gremlin, a messy bunch of minus signs wandering about inside the hazard rate key function. I think this code produces a result that passes the sense check.
>
> gz<-function(z,
>              beta, sigintercept, sigcoef, DistWin,
>              key="HR", w=max(z)){
>   #this is a generic detection function that returns the probability of detecting an animal
>   #    z               generic distance (perpendicular) - can be scalar or vector
>   #    beta            shape coefficient
>   #    sigmaintercept  intercept coefficient for sigma
>   #    sigcoef         coefficient for specific factor level
>   #    DistWin         coefficients from Distance for Windows or from R
>   #    key             the detection function key, only works for hazard rate
>   #    w               truncation distance, by default the max of the distances
>   #
>   #RETURNS: a probability
>
>   if(key=="HR") {
>     if (DistWin) {
>       sigma <- sigintercept + exp(sigcoef)
>       exponent <- beta
>     } else {
>       sigma <- exp(sigintercept + sigcoef)
>       exponent <- exp(beta)
>     }
>     scale.dist <- z/sigma
>     inside <- -(scale.dist)^(-exponent)
>     gx <- 1 - exp(inside)
>   }
>   return(gx)
> }
>
> maxz <- 800
> betaval <- 0.4142978
> sigint <- 5.4885488
>
> beaustates <- c("State 0","State 1", "State 2", "State 3", "State 4")
> beaucoeff <- c(0, -0.3979885, -0.5518057, -0.8339985, -1.3146111)
> esw <- vector(mode="numeric", length=length(beaustates))
> for (i in 1:length(beaustates)) {
>   esw[i] <- integrate(gz, 0, maxz,
>                       beta=betaval, sigintercept = sigint, sigcoef = beaucoeff[i],  DistWin=FALSE)$value
>   if(i==1) {
>     plot(seq(0,maxz),
>          gz(beta=betaval, sigintercept = sigint, sigcoef = beaucoeff[i], z=seq(0,maxz), DistWin=FALSE),
>          lwd=3, type="l", col=i, main="Detection functions by sea state",
>          xlab="Distance", ylab="Detection probability", ylim=c(0,1))
>   } else {
>     lines(seq(0,maxz),
>           gz(beta=betaval, sigintercept = sigint, sigcoef = beaucoeff[i], z=seq(0,maxz), DistWin=FALSE),
>           lwd=3, type="l", col=i)
>   }
> }
> msg <- paste(beaustates, title="Estimated ESW", round(esw, 1))
> legend("topright", legend=msg, lwd=2, col=1:5)
>
> From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Tim Awbery <tim.a...@sams.ac.uk>
> Sent: 12 May 2023 16:51
>
> To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] p and esw for each value of covariat
>
> Hi,
>
>
>
> Thanks for your prompt response and for the provided code.
>
> The function appears to run, and I am able to reproduce the figure above with no problem.
>
>
>
> By my calculations, my ESW for the overall model is: mu = W * Pa  = 800 * 0.41 = 331.43 metres.
>
> I would therefore expect my ESW in lower sea states to be greater than this and vice versa in higher sea states.
>
>  However, when I substitute in my model intercept, scale coefficients and shape coefficient, even at a Sea State of zero, my ESW is only 217 metres with the ESW reduced to 58 metres at a Sea State of 5.
>
>  Additionally, the functions appear to have a much smaller shoulder compared to the original model. I thought I understood which values needed replacing (please see attached) but now I am less sure.
>
>
>
> If you’re able to provide any confirmation or correction regarding this, then I’d be very grateful.
>
> I have attached the output figure provided by yours and Tiago’s code as well as the shape of the original model and my edited code, in case it is of any help in diagnosing my mistake.
>
>
>
> Thank you in advance.
>
>
>
> Best,
>
>
>
> Tim

> On Thursday, May 11, 2023 at 2:06:50 PM UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Tim
> >
> > A bit of a mess with code to do some fiddly calculations in answer to your questions; borrowing some code from my colleague Tiago along the way.  Need to extract estimated coefficients, place them into the hazard rate key function, integrate said function over the appropriate range to get ESW (according to this formula):
> >
> > Code has not been checked to ensure its integrity, but it seems to give reasonable results.  Note the coefficients for sea states 1 and 2 are virtually identical, hence the two detection function curves live atop one another in this plot:
> >
> > gz<-function(z,

messages.body_plain:
Rebecca

Not to worry. Think about "CoveredArea" in this way: it is the area sampled taking into account multiple visits to the transect.

Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. If detectability is pefect, what is an estimate of beetle density from that survey? It is the total number of beetles (20) divided by the area sampled. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.

We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.

The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:

The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):

How was that estimate derived:

Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9

Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area

Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion

Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area

Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare

Does this relieve your anxiety?

An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.

messages.body_plain:
Thomas

I'm trying to decide if you need bespoke code or whether existing code can do what you want.

The "average p" provided in the summary you presented is the probability of detection from 0 to the truncation distance. For visualisation, there is the function "add_df_covar_line" that works for point transects to see the effect of covariate levels on detectability.

Investigate those avenues and they are not suitable for your needs you might be able to adapt "add_df_covar_line" for your needs. Let me know.

Eventually combining it with either other recording sites, or detection thresholds, or background noise to provide a visual comaprison of how these change the probability of detection, similar to the above plot when using sea state as a factor.

Im assuming I would need to update the gz function to work with point sampled data, but I'm unsure of the correct equation.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Best,
Thomas

Hi there,
That was very helpful thank you so much for your response. Would I therefore be correct in saying that the effort is the number of points per area x number of visits to the points (does the amount of time surveying at each point come in anywhere?).
Thanks again,
Rebecca

On Tue, Oct 1, 2024 at 2:19 AM Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> Rebecca
>
> Not to worry. Think about "CoveredArea" in this way: it is the area sampled taking into account multiple visits to the transect.
>
> Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. If detectability is pefect, what is an estimate of beetle density from that survey? It is the total number of beetles (20) divided by the area sampled. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.
>
> We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
> Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
> Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.
>
> The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:
>
>
> The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):
>
>
> How was that estimate derived:
>
> Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9
>
> Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area
>
> Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion
>
> Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
> Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area
>
> Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare
>
> Does this relieve your anxiety?
>
> An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.
>

messages.body_plain:
Rebecca

Duration of a point count visit (5min, 10min, ...) is only relevant if performing avian cue counting surveys where a detection is of a "song" rather than an animal. Distance sampling can then be used to estimate "song" density in units of songs/area/time. Then a "song production rate" multiplier (measured in units of songs per time) is applied to convert song density into bird density.

Hi there,
That was very helpful thank you so much for your response. Would I therefore be correct in saying that the effort is the number of points per area x number of visits to the points (does the amount of time surveying at each point come in anywhere?).
Thanks again,
Rebecca

On Tue, Oct 1, 2024 at 2:19 AM Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> Rebecca
>
> Not to worry. Think about "CoveredArea" in this way: it is the area sampled taking into account multiple visits to the transect.
>
> Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. If detectability is pefect, what is an estimate of beetle density from that survey? It is the total number of beetles (20) divided by the area sampled. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.
>
> We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
> Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357.  https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
> Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.
>
> The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:
>
>
> The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):
>
>
> How was that estimate derived:
>
> Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9
>
> Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area
>
> Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion
>
> Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
> Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area
>
> Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare
>
> Does this relieve your anxiety?
>
> An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.

messages.body_plain:
Adding to Eric’s comment, the method he describes is the cue-count method.  In standard point transect sampling, conceptually, recording at a point is a ‘snapshot’ – that is, instantaneous.  The method gives upwardly-biased density estimates if birds are moving around during the period spent recording at a point.  For a discussion of this issue and how to avoid this bias, see

Buckland, S.T. 2006.  Point transect surveys for songbirds:  robust methodologies.  The Auk 123, 345-357.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.body_plain:
Thank you both for your help. I am indeed looking at recording bird song (hence why sample is limited by number of recording devices) but will take each song as an individual by cutting repeat species calls within the same 5 minute period. Since each call will thus be assumed to represent an individual would it be okay to maintain the original method rather than the cue counting method? Additionally, for repeats of an individual should the first call or the average call distance be taken?
Kind regards, Rebecca

> On 2 Oct 2024, at 02:52, Stephen Buckland <st...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Adding to Eric’s comment, the method he describes is the cue-count method.  In standard point transect sampling, conceptually, recording at a point is a ‘snapshot’ – that is, instantaneous.  The method gives upwardly-biased density estimates if birds are moving around during the period spent recording at a point.  For a discussion of this issue and how to avoid this bias, see
>
> Buckland, S.T. 2006.  Point transect surveys for songbirds:  robust methodologies.  The Auk 123, 345-357.
>
>
>
> Steve Buckland
>
>
>
> From: 'Eric Rexstad' via distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Sent: 02 October 2024 07:52
> To: Rebecca MacArthur <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> Cc: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
>
>
>
> Rebecca
>
>
>
> Duration of a point count visit (5min, 10min, ...) is only relevant if performing avian cue counting surveys where a detection is of a "song" rather than an animal. Distance sampling can then be used to estimate "song" density in units of songs/area/time. Then a "song production rate" multiplier (measured in units of songs per time) is applied to convert song density into bird density.
>
> From: Rebecca MacArthur <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> Sent: 02 October 2024 01:35
> To: Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk>
> Cc: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
>
>

> Hi there,
>
> That was very helpful thank you so much for your response. Would I therefore be correct in saying that the effort is the number of points per area x number of visits to the points (does the amount of time surveying at each point come in anywhere?).
>
> Thanks again,
>
> Rebecca
>
>

> On Tue, Oct 1, 2024 at 2:19 AM Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

> > Rebecca
> >
> >
> >
> > Not to worry. Think about "CoveredArea" in this way: it is the area sampled taking into account multiple visits to the transect.
> >
> >
> >
> > Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. If detectability is pefect, what is an estimate of beetle density from that survey? It is the total number of beetles (20) divided by the area sampled. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.
> >
> >
> >
> > We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
> > Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
> >
> > Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.
> >
> >
> >
> > The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:
> >
> >

> > <image001.png>

> >
> >
> > The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):
> >
> >

> > <image002.png>

> >
> >
> > How was that estimate derived:
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area
> >
> >
> >
> > Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion
> >
> >
> >
> > Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
> >
> > Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare
> >
> >
> >
> > Does this relieve your anxiety?
> >
> >
> >
> > An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.
> >
> >
> >
> > From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Rebecca <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> > Sent: 30 September 2024 20:35
> > To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> > Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
> >
> >

> > To add another question for the same R script (above was talking about input file for ds), for my dht2 output the 'Area' is coming out as the individual area for each region whereas the 'CoveredArea' is presented as the total, meaning my abundance estimates are lower than the actual sample since the covered area is greater than the total.

> > <image003.png>

> > >
> > > Hi there,
> > >
> > > I believe I am having a similar issue. I am carrying out a point transect survey with 4 points, each visited 80 times. I put my effort for each observation as 80 but the covered area has been calculated by multiplying the area of each point by 80 - I assume this is because it is assuming I have sampled 80 points per area (4 areas) whereas each area is only 1 point and repeats were at the same location meaning the covered area is 80x too large.
> > >
> > > Hope you can help!
> > >
> > > Thank you,
> > >
> > > Rebecca
> > >
> > > On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 2:02:07 AM UTC-6 er26 wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Exactly right Cali.  The "Survey effort" field is a mandatory field (visits for points, line length for transects).  Distance MUST have that information because it is "hard wired" into Distance's calculations.  Therefore, you need not explicitly "point" to that field, Distance looks for it automatically.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >

> > > > >
> > > > > hi Eric, thanks for the quick replay.
> > > > >
> > > > > So if I understand what you're saying, simply by specifying survey effort in the data import stage, I've done all I need to do. I don't need to refer to that column indicating survey effort in any of the further model input windows. Is that right? Great!
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks
> > > > >
> > > > > Cali
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, Oct 1, 2015 at 9:46 PM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cali
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Not sure I understand your question.  Sounds like you've set up your project properly.  You have recorded number of visits in the "Survey effort" field of the transect layer along with covariates (including visit number) at the observation layer.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Distance calculates encounter rate as the number of detections per unit of effort (visit).  Consequently by specifying 3 visits to the point, Distance calculates the proper encounter rate.  There is no need for the number of visits to be equal for all points.  Perhaps on one visit, you were unable to get to some of the points, therefore the number of detections on those points will be a function of 2 visits rather than 3; you merely indicate "Survey effort" of 2 for those points.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your analysis will not model survey effort (it is known and not estimated), but the number of detections is a function of effort; that is taken into account in the manner I described.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On 02/10/2015 02:50,  ca...@kauaiforestbirds.org wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > hi all, I've seen several related posts but so far none that answer my question.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > We have made three visits over the course of several weeks to each of 30 point count stations, where we performed an 8-minute count on each visit.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > We have imported all of the data into Distance, accounting for the three repeat visits as "survey effort" at the "point transect" level. So for each point, we have the name of the point, and the survey effort = 3. Then at the sample level, we have each observation with its distance, as well as covariates relating to the time and weather of each visit, and the visit number (1-3).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My question is: where in the modeling phase (the "inputs") do we bring the survey effort in? i.e., where do we tell Distance that we have repeated counts at each station, as opposed to all of those observations coming from a single visit.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I understand that the point may be moot because we have equal numbers of visits at all stations....but even if so, for the future, when that is likely to not be the case, I'd like to know how to model survey effort.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks!
> > > > > > > Cali

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.body_plain:
Rebecca

I don't understand what you mean about "cutting repeated species calls". If you are taking the cue counting approach (which you must be doing if using autonomous recorders rather than human observers), you record each call as a  detection and you measure distances (you don't describe how you are doing this) for each and every call.  Cue counting makes no assumptions about calls belonging to individuals.

Regarding your next email, you need to measure cue production rate for a number of individuals (because all individuals do not produce cues at the same rate). You then need to measure the variability in call rates between individuals to incorporate variability in call production rate at the population level as part of uncertainty in your estimates of density. Have a look at one of the distance sampling text books to understand all the components that go into estimating animal density from cue counts.
From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Rebecca MacArthur <rmaca...@gmail.com>
Sent: 02 October 2024 14:39
To: Stephen Buckland <st...@st-andrews.ac.uk>
Cc: Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk>; distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>

Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance

Thank you both for your help. I am indeed looking at recording bird song (hence why sample is limited by number of recording devices) but will take each song as an individual by cutting repeat species calls within the same 5 minute period. Since each call will thus be assumed to represent an individual would it be okay to maintain the original method rather than the cue counting method? Additionally, for repeats of an individual should the first call or the average call distance be taken?
Kind regards, Rebecca

> On 2 Oct 2024, at 02:52, Stephen Buckland <st...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> ﻿
>
> Adding to Eric’s comment, the method he describes is the cue-count method.  In standard point transect sampling, conceptually, recording at a point is a ‘snapshot’ – that is, instantaneous.  The method gives upwardly-biased density estimates if birds are moving around during the period spent recording at a point.  For a discussion of this issue and how to avoid this bias, see
>
> Buckland, S.T. 2006.  Point transect surveys for songbirds:  robust methodologies.  The Auk 123, 345-357.
>
>
>
> Steve Buckland
>
>
>
> From: 'Eric Rexstad' via distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Sent: 02 October 2024 07:52
> To: Rebecca MacArthur <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> Cc: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
>
>
>
> Rebecca
>
>
>
> Duration of a point count visit (5min, 10min, ...) is only relevant if performing avian cue counting surveys where a detection is of a "song" rather than an animal. Distance sampling can then be used to estimate "song" density in units of songs/area/time. Then a "song production rate" multiplier (measured in units of songs per time) is applied to convert song density into bird density.
>
> From: Rebecca MacArthur <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> Sent: 02 October 2024 01:35
> To: Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk>
> Cc: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
>
>
>
> Hi there,
>
> That was very helpful thank you so much for your response. Would I therefore be correct in saying that the effort is the number of points per area x number of visits to the points (does the amount of time surveying at each point come in anywhere?).
>
> Thanks again,
>
> Rebecca
>
>
>
> On Tue, Oct 1, 2024 at 2:19 AM Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> >
> > Rebecca
> >
> >
> >
> > Not to worry. Think about "CoveredArea" in this way: it is the area sampled taking into account multiple visits to the transect.
> >
> >
> >
> > Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. If detectability is pefect, what is an estimate of beetle density from that survey? It is the total number of beetles (20) divided by the area sampled. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.
> >
> >
> >
> > We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
> > Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357.  https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
> >
> > Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.
> >
> >
> >
> > The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:
> >
> >
> >
> > <image001.png>
> >
> >
> >
> > The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):
> >
> >
> >
> > <image002.png>
> >
> >
> >
> > How was that estimate derived:
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area
> >
> >
> >
> > Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion
> >
> >
> >
> > Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
> >
> > Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area
> >
> >
> >
> > Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare
> >
> >
> >
> > Does this relieve your anxiety?
> >
> >
> >
> > An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.
> >
> >
> >
> > From: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Rebecca <rmaca...@gmail.com>
> > Sent: 30 September 2024 20:35
> > To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
> > Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
> >
> >
> >
> > To add another question for the same R script (above was talking about input file for ds), for my dht2 output the 'Area' is coming out as the individual area for each region whereas the 'CoveredArea' is presented as the total, meaning my abundance estimates are lower than the actual sample since the covered area is greater than the total.
> > <image003.png>
> >
> > On Monday, September 30, 2024 at 12:25:17 PM UTC-6 Rebecca wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi there,
> > >
> > > I believe I am having a similar issue. I am carrying out a point transect survey with 4 points, each visited 80 times. I put my effort for each observation as 80 but the covered area has been calculated by multiplying the area of each point by 80 - I assume this is because it is assuming I have sampled 80 points per area (4 areas) whereas each area is only 1 point and repeats were at the same location meaning the covered area is 80x too large.
> > >
> > > Hope you can help!
> > >
> > > Thank you,
> > >
> > > Rebecca
> > >
> > > On Friday, October 2, 2015 at 2:02:07 AM UTC-6 er26 wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Exactly right Cali.  The "Survey effort" field is a mandatory field (visits for points, line length for transects).  Distance MUST have that information because it is "hard wired" into Distance's calculations.  Therefore, you need not explicitly "point" to that field, Distance looks for it automatically.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On 02/10/2015 08:56, Lisa Cali Crampton wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > hi Eric, thanks for the quick replay.
> > > > >
> > > > > So if I understand what you're saying, simply by specifying survey effort in the data import stage, I've done all I need to do. I don't need to refer to that column indicating survey effort in any of the further model input windows. Is that right? Great!
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks
> > > > >
> > > > > Cali
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, Oct 1, 2015 at 9:46 PM, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cali
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Not sure I understand your question.  Sounds like you've set up your project properly.  You have recorded number of visits in the "Survey effort" field of the transect layer along with covariates (including visit number) at the observation layer.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Distance calculates encounter rate as the number of detections per unit of effort (visit).  Consequently by specifying 3 visits to the point, Distance calculates the proper encounter rate.  There is no need for the number of visits to be equal for all points.  Perhaps on one visit, you were unable to get to some of the points, therefore the number of detections on those points will be a function of 2 visits rather than 3; you merely indicate "Survey effort" of 2 for those points.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your analysis will not model survey effort (it is known and not estimated), but the number of detections is a function of effort; that is taken into account in the manner I described.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On 02/10/2015 02:50,  ca...@kauaiforestbirds.org wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > hi all, I've seen several related posts but so far none that answer my question.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > We have made three visits over the course of several weeks to each of 30 point count stations, where we performed an 8-minute count on each visit.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > We have imported all of the data into Distance, accounting for the three repeat visits as "survey effort" at the "point transect" level. So for each point, we have the name of the point, and the survey effort = 3. Then at the sample level, we have each observation with its distance, as well as covariates relating to the time and weather of each visit, and the visit number (1-3).
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My question is: where in the modeling phase (the "inputs") do we bring the survey effort in? i.e., where do we tell Distance that we have repeated counts at each station, as opposed to all of those observations coming from a single visit.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I understand that the point may be moot because we have equal numbers of visits at all stations....but even if so, for the future, when that is likely to not be the case, I'd like to know how to model survey effort.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance
messages.body_plain:
You would input the cue rate as the average (across the monitored individuals) and standard error, rather than enter each monitored individual.  For the individuals that you include in your cue rate estimation, you need to be able to detect all songbursts (or calls) within the time that you monitor them.  Try reading up on the method, either in the 2006 Auk paper, or the 2015 distance sampling book.  The book covers more issues, so would be the better option.  I’ll send you off-list the Auk paper.

Steve Buckland

Thank you Eric, would I therefore be correct in saying that if the same species was heard making 5 calls in a 5-minute period it would be taken as 1 individual with a cue rate of 1 and this is repeated for every individual and an average and SE taken for each species? The input data would therefore have a list of every individual with the average cue rate for the species and the distance from the recorder.

If you are taking the cue counting approach (which you must be doing if using autonomous recorders rather than human observers), you record each call as a  detection and you measure distances (you don't describe how you are doing this) for each and every call.  Cue counting makes no assumptions about calls belonging to individuals.
>
>
>
> Regarding your next email, you need to measure cue production rate for a number of individuals (because all individuals do not produce cues at the same rate). You then need to measure the variability in call rates between individuals to incorporate variability in call production rate at the population level as part of uncertainty in your estimates of density. Have a look at one of the distance sampling text books to understand all the components that go into estimating animal density from cue counts.

messages.subject: How does the dsm function link the ddf.obj and the observation data?

messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance Samplers,

I'm working on a DSM to look at seabird habitat associations using R. I have a question about the mechanics of how the dsm function links observations to the detection function. I have a small number of observations for one species (n=49) and a larger number of detections of a second, similar species (n= ~250). Biologically, I think it is reasonable to lump the two species for fitting a combined detection function which I would then use for my dsm to estimate density of the rarer species.

My specific question is how the dsm function deals with observations in the detection function that are not linked through the object column to the observations data frame. The model runs but I'm struggling to figure out if it's actually doing what I hope it's doing. So, can I use observations in the detection function that I don't use in the observation data frame?

Any insights would be appreciated,
Brendan

messages.body_plain:
Brendan

I don't have first-hand experience with what you are attempting to accomplish. I suspect the route to addressing your issue lies with taking the "multiddf" route.

The "ddf.obj" argument to the "dsm()" function can take a list of fitted detection function objects; in your case those could be detection functions for the different species. This way you need not make the assumption that the species share a common detection function.

This methodology is described in
Miller DL, Fifield D, Wakefield E, Sigourney DB. 2021. Extending density surface models to include multiple and double-observer survey data. PeerJ 9:e12113  https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.12113
The authors helpfully provide Rmarkdown vignettes of the analyses in the papers here:
All code and data are available at Zenodo: DL Miller. (2021). dill/multiddf-supp-materials: Code version for revision of the paper. (paper-revision). Zenodo.  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5116140.
See if that approach may be useful to you.

Hello Distance Samplers,

I'm working on a DSM to look at seabird habitat associations using R. I have a question about the mechanics of how the dsm function links observations to the detection function. I have a small number of observations for one species (n=49) and a larger number of detections of a second, similar species (n= ~250). Biologically, I think it is reasonable to lump the two species for fitting a combined detection function which I would then use for my dsm to estimate density of the rarer species.

My specific question is how the dsm function deals with observations in the detection function that are not linked through the object column to the observations data frame. The model runs but I'm struggling to figure out if it's actually doing what I hope it's doing. So, can I use observations in the detection function that I don't use in the observation data frame?

Any insights would be appreciated,
Brendan

Adding to that, how you define a cue depends on the species.  In my case, for three of the species, it was a ‘songburst’ – a single bout of song followed by a period of silence.  In the case of the European robin, its song can go on for an extended period, but it is made up of song ‘phrases’, so each phrase was taken as a cue.  That explains the higher cue rate for that species.  Carrion crows in the UK typically give 3 calls in quick succession, so if I was applying the method to them, I would take the set of 3 calls to be a single cue.

Steve Buckland

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Take this fictious example: I visit a square meter of ground and count 11 beetles in that square meter. Tomorrow I visit the same square meter again and count 9 beetles. I would argue that the area sampled is 2m^2, making the density estimate 10 beetles per m^2.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > We can follow these calculations with a point transect survey with multiple visits. Use the data set "wren_snapshot" that ships with the Distance package. It represents an analysis published in
> > > > > Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357.  https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345
> > > > >
> > > > > Thirty two point transects were visited two times and the data were truncated at 110m. One hundred seventeen (117) detections of winter wrens were made by Prof Buckland.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > The result of a fitted hazard rate model is summarised below:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > <image001.png>
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > The density estimate (1.023) is the same as published in Buckland (2006):
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > <image002.png>
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > How was that estimate derived:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Estimated birds in the covered area = birds detected / detection probability = 117/0.47 = 248.9
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Estimated density = estimated birds in covered area / covered area
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Covered area = number points * number visits * pi * (truncation distance)^2 / (meters per hectare) # unit conversion
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Covered area = 32 points * 2 visits * 3.14159 * (110m)^2 / 10000
> > > > >
> > > > > Covered area = 243.28 hectares # note this covered area is much larger than the size of the study area
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Estimated density = 248.9 birds / 243.28 hectares = 1.02 birds per hectare
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Does this relieve your anxiety?
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Temporal replication (repeated visits) is not a substitute for spatial replication. Encounter rate variance (one component of uncertainty in density estimation) is computed on the basis of variability between spatial replicates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.

Rebecca

The cue rate value depends upon the duration over which the cue rate is measured. Prof Buckland conducted his cue counts for 5 minutes, hence the cue rate per 5 minutes is 7.28. Expressed as number of cues per minute, the value is 1.456.

messages.body_snippet:
Rebecca

The cue rate value depends upon the duration over which the cue rate is measured. Prof Buckland conducted his cue counts for 5 minutes, hence the cue rate per 5 minutes is 7.28. Expressed as

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] how to analyze repeated point counts in Distance

messages.body_plain:
I believe that the rate in the paper is cues per 5mins, which was the time spent at each point.  The rate in the example will be the rate per minute.  Effort would be number of 5-min periods in the first case, and number of minutes in the second.  Both ways of analysing the data will give the same estimate.

You must record cue rate for a representative sample of birds.  Do not record just when they’re singing – it must be an average across birds.  If for example you’re estimating number of territories of a songbird, with an assumed 1 male per territory, you would need to select a representative sample of territories, and record for a pre-determined time period.  That doesn’t need to be a long time period.  Because different individuals may have different cue rates, monitoring a number of birds, each for a short period, is preferable to monitoring a few birds, each for a long period.

________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Additionally, when determining cue rate, should I record for a full hour and then divide by 60 to get the cues per minute (meaning less commonly heard species would have a lower cue rate) or just count cues made whilst singing?

Many thanks again,

Rebecca

>
> I believe that the rate in the paper is cues per 5mins, which was the time spent at each point.  The rate in the example will be the rate per minute.  Effort would be number of 5-min periods in the first case, and number of minutes in the second.  Both ways of analysing the data will give the same estimate.
>
>
>
> You must record cue rate for a representative sample of birds.  Do not record just when they’re singing – it must be an average across birds.  If for example you’re estimating number of territories of a songbird, with an assumed 1 male per territory, you would need to select a representative sample of territories, and record for a pre-determined time period.  That doesn’t need to be a long time period.  Because different individuals may have different cue rates, monitoring a number of birds, each for a short period, is preferable to monitoring a few birds, each for a long period.
>

> > > > > > An aside: having 4 replicate point transects (spatial replicates) visited 80 times is not going to produce terribly robust estimates. Having a small number of spatial replicates leads to poor estimates of this encounter rate variance. A better survey design to employ in the future is to have more spatial replicates visited fewer times, resulting in more reliable estimates with effectively the same sampling effort.

messages.body_plain:
Alvaro

You have animals that occur in groups (flocks). In your data frame "bd_trans_Distance", you must have a column specifically named "size", where you provide the number of animals in each detected flock.

By providing a column with that reserved name "size", the "ds()" function knows to estimate both the abundance of flocks and the abundance of individuals (where estimated abundance of individuals is the estimated abundance of flocks multiplied by the average size of observed flocks).  This estimate is often biased because small flocks at distance are absent from the sample, therefore the average size of observed flocks is greater than the average size of flocks in the population.

This can be remedied by using "size" as a covariate in the detection function.

Hope that helps.

You're right, Eric, I found it in the ds function documentation.

I have run the ds function with 3 different configurations:

1 -) with my database with a "size" column:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,

+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5497.912
Estimate: 559

2 -) without "size" column:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,

+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5497.912
Estimate: 210

3 -) without "size" column in my database but including flock size (as "num") as a covariate:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,

+                   key = "hn",
+                   formula=~num,
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5498.913
Estimate: 210

The AICs I've received have been virtually identical although density estimates vary considerably. Does it mean that there are no biases in my data or that they do not substantially affect the results?

Thank you so much!
Alvaro

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] number of iindividuals in each detection
messages.body_plain:
Alvaro

If you recorded detections of groups, then your data frame must include size; otherwise the ds() function is producing an estimate of the abundance of groups, not abundance of individuals. Therefore your analyses 2 and 3 are not doing what you want (estimating abundance of individuals).

To adjust for possible size bias in your estimation, in addition to method 1) also fit another model:

Distance.hn.sizecov <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   formula=~size

+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)

Perform AIC comparison of those two models to determine if size affects detectability.

From: Alvaro G <alvar...@gmail.com>
Sent: 17 October 2024 08:32
To: Eric Rexstad <Eric.R...@st-andrews.ac.uk>
Cc: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>

Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] number of iindividuals in each detection

You're right, Eric, I found it in the ds function documentation.

I have run the ds function with 3 different configurations:

1 -) with my database with a "size" column:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5497.912
Estimate: 559

2 -) without "size" column:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5497.912
Estimate: 210

3 -) without "size" column in my database but including flock size (as "num") as a covariate:

> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
+                   key = "hn",
+                   formula=~num,
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5498.913
Estimate: 210

The AICs I've received have been virtually identical although density estimates vary considerably. Does it mean that there are no biases in my data or that they do not substantially affect the results?

Thank you so much!
Alvaro

I'm just wondering if you then have a visit where no bird was seen, should you still include an observation row with the same accumulated effort and transect details, but with blank species and distance columns ?

Thanks,
Colin

messages.subject_clean: Assistance with DSM Data Formatting for Curved Transects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I hope this is the right place to reach out with a question about Density Surface Models. If not, would you be able to direct me to someone who might be able to help?

My question concerns the segmentation of transects using the function segs <- st_segmentize(transects, dfMaxLength=units::set_units(2000, "metres")). Unlike the example found here `dsm` data formatting example <https://examples.distancesampling.org/dsm-data-formatting/dsm-data-formatting.html> , my transects are not straight lines due to the complex area we surveyed in the northern GBRMP. This function is producing very short segments, which may affect subsequent analysis by resulting in an excess of small segments and a large number of rows linking to observations.
We suspect this may be due to the curved nature of our transects. When I manually adjust the transects to be straighter, the segment lengths approach the truncation distance (doubled) more closely. However, this might bias the sample.

Should I continuing with the actual curved transects despite the small segments, or might another function yield more uniform segment lengths? Alternatively, could I use GIS software for segmentation be a viable solution, or is there a different approach for these type of transects?

Thank you for taking the time to consider my questions.

Valeria

Welcome to the list.

Appreciate you providing a bit of your data so I could diagnose your problem. You don't indicate whether the survey you conducted was lines or points; I'll presume lines, but the answer to that question does not influence the problem you are having.

I think the reason R might be offering a complaint is because of the use of "," as the decimal separator in your Area, Effort and distance fields. Adding the argument "dec" to the "read.table" function resolves this issue. I make a file named "elena.txt" from the lines of data you sent and wrote the following few lines of code, running the code did not generate the warning about a missing "distbegin" column.

mydata <- read.table("E:/troubleshoot/Elena/elena.txt", header=TRUE,  dec=",")
library(Distance)
test <- ds(data = mydata, key="hn")
summary(test)
plot(test)

Hopefully that solves your problem and you can carry on with your analyses.  Let us know if anything else arises.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 I’m performing distance analysis to obtain density estimates for a species in R using the ds() function. I have raw data of the following form:

Region.Label / Sample.Label / Effort / FieldLabel / Habitat / distbegin / distend / Count

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25      1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100      5
BR22 1 80 A Arable 100 200      NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 0 25      1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 25 100      NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200      2
BR22 2 120 C Arable 0 25      NA
BR22 2 120 C Arable 25 100      NA
BR22 2 120 C Arable 100 200      NA

I first make each count into a single row (e.g. there will be five identical rows for location BR22, transect 1, field A, distbegin 25, distend 100), but then I am not exactly sure how to deal with the NA rows. I have put two possibilities below.

Data for ds() model in R (version 1): in this version I ignore the NA rows for transect 1, fields A and B as we have counts from other distance bins, and I include one NA row for transect 2, field C:

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25         1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100         1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100    1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100         1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 0 25     1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200  1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200  1
BR22 2 120 C Arable NA NA         NA

Data for ds() model in R (version 2): in this version I include NA rows for transect 1, fields A and B to account for the NAs from certain distance bands, and I include one NA row for transect 2, field C:

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25    1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100  1
BR22 1 80 A Arable NA NA    NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 0 25    1
BR22 1 80 B Grass NA NA   NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200   1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200  1
BR22 2 120 C Arable NA NA          NA

My feeling is that version 1 would be the correct way to deal with the NA observations, but I’m second guessing myself now! Any help and advice will be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,

Charlotte.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Dealing with NA observations and binned analyses
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Dealing with NA observations and binned analyses
messages.body_plain:
Charlotte

Thanks for your question. Your instinct (believing version 1 to be correct) is accurate.

The "ds" function is deriving two distinct pieces of information from the data frame provided to it: a) information about distances (in your case bins) to detected objects and b) (equally important) information about survey design. It is through the use of NAs that complete information about the survey design is passed to "ds".

By referring to "survey design" what I mean is information about numbers of strata, transects within strata and effort associated with those transects. Note, that I do not include "distance bins" as relating to "survey design". Those bins only serve a purpose in the detection function model fitting. Hence, there is no need to have an entry in the data frame for each bin of each transect (as you show in your original table).  Therefore, your "verison 1" data frame contains necessary information about the survey design; with the row for transect 2 in field C. That row must exist for complete survey design information to be available to "ds". However, without detections on that transect, the fields distbegin, distend and count need to be populated with NA.

As an aside, I see in your "version 0", you have count values >= 1, whereas for your "version 1" data frame, you have changed transect 1 of stratum A to be five detections of single birds within the 25-100 bin. These are two ways of dealing with animals that occur in groups; the two approaches should produce equivalent estimates, see
Buckland, S.T., Plumptre, A.J., Thomas, L. et al. Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates. Int J Primatol 31, 833–847 (2010). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5

Hi all,

 I’m performing distance analysis to obtain density estimates for a species in R using the ds() function. I have raw data of the following form:

Region.Label / Sample.Label / Effort / FieldLabel / Habitat / distbegin / distend / Count

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25      1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100      5
BR22 1 80 A Arable 100 200      NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 0 25      1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 25 100      NA
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200      2
BR22 2 120 C Arable 0 25      NA
BR22 2 120 C Arable 25 100      NA
BR22 2 120 C Arable 100 200      NA

I first make each count into a single row (e.g. there will be five identical rows for location BR22, transect 1, field A, distbegin 25, distend 100), but then I am not exactly sure how to deal with the NA rows. I have put two possibilities below.

Data for ds() model in R (version 1): in this version I ignore the NA rows for transect 1, fields A and B as we have counts from other distance bins, and I include one NA row for transect 2, field C:

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25         1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100         1

BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100 1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100         1

BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200 1
BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200 1
BR22 2 120 C Arable NA NA         NA

Data for ds() model in R (version 2): in this version I include NA rows for transect 1, fields A and B to account for the NAs from certain distance bands, and I include one NA row for transect 2, field C:

BR22 1 80 A Arable 0 25    1
BR22 1 80 A Arable 25 100 1

BR22 1 80 B Grass 100 200 1
BR22 2 120 C Arable NA NA          NA

My feeling is that version 1 would be the correct way to deal with the NA observations, but I’m second guessing myself now! Any help and advice will be greatly appreciated.

Thank you,

Charlotte.

On Thursday 31 October 2024 at 10:41:43 UTC Eric Rexstad wrote:
> Charlotte
>
> Thanks for your question. Your instinct (believing version 1 to be correct) is accurate.
>
> The "ds" function is deriving two distinct pieces of information from the data frame provided to it: a) information about distances (in your case bins) to detected objects and b) (equally important) information about survey design. It is through the use of NAs that complete information about the survey design is passed to "ds".
>
> By referring to "survey design" what I mean is information about numbers of strata, transects within strata and effort associated with those transects. Note, that I do not include "distance bins" as relating to "survey design". Those bins only serve a purpose in the detection function model fitting. Hence, there is no need to have an entry in the data frame for each bin of each transect (as you show in your original table).  Therefore, your "verison 1" data frame contains necessary information about the survey design; with the row for transect 2 in field C. That row must exist for complete survey design information to be available to "ds". However, without detections on that transect, the fields distbegin, distend and count need to be populated with NA.
>
> As an aside, I see in your "version 0", you have count values >= 1, whereas for your "version 1" data frame, you have changed transect 1 of stratum A to be five detections of single birds within the 25-100 bin. These are two ways of dealing with animals that occur in groups; the two approaches should produce equivalent estimates, see
